title: SchwingCheck ML Report
heading: Naming vertebral levels from measurements: the ML view
lede: A generative Bayesian classifier names which lumbar level a run of measured vertebral bodies sits at. Its parameters are per-level means and SDs read from published tables, never fitted by gradient. This page evaluates it the way a classifier is evaluated: held-out populations as the test set, log loss and top-1 accuracy as the metrics, calibration checked, hyperparameters set by nested cross-validation, and the best variant chosen on held-out predictive performance alone, as the owner asked on 2026-10-30.
meta: The stats view of the same records, with every table and the full prose, is the other page and the README; this one restates its findings in ML terms and adds the model-selection study of 2026-10-30. Everything is synthetic but the papers' numbers: no grid, no WSU data, no scan.
tiles: plain to tempered (T = 2); the oracle, the population's own table, is 0.590
ECE of the top probability, plain to tempered; widened by tau 0.042, mixture 0.086
plain to the mixture, the only gain, within one SE; the oracle is 72.4%
task:
**Task.** Multi-class classification. The input is a field: B adjacent vertebral bodies (B = 1, 2 or 3) with M measurements each (lengths in mm, areas in mm2, angles in degrees; M is 1 to 15 depending on which measures the population prints). The label is the field's starting level in the lumbar run L1 to L5, so there are K = 6 - B classes. A chance classifier scores 1/K.

**Model.** A generative classifier, not a discriminative one. Under class k each measure's B values are jointly Gaussian: a patient has a latent size s shared by every measure (one factor), the mean of measure m at level l is s mu[m, l], and the covariance is diagonal plus a rank-one term from the size, which gives a closed-form log likelihood. The size is integrated out by 161-node Gauss-Hermite quadrature over log s ~ N(0, 0.07^2), measures multiply (conditional independence given the size and the place), and the posterior over classes is exact Bayes with a uniform prior. There is no gradient training: the parameters are the tables mu and sd, one mean and one SD per measure and level, read from the literature. The code is schwingcheck/rule.py; the vectorised likelihood is one batched matrix product.

**Training data.** The 39 papers of the clinical reread, each giving per-level means and SDs (sufficient statistics, never raw rows), pooled per cell by a random-effects meta-analysis: a hierarchical model with one latent mean per population and a between-population variance tau^2 estimated by REML. The pool is the training set; a single paper is one population drawn from the hierarchy.

**Test data.** Real raw measurements are not available in this repository, so the test set is synthetic: patients are sampled from the held-out paper's own means and SDs through the same generative model (schwingcheck's generator, validated against the papers in the simulator section below). The test distribution is therefore a population the classifier has never seen, with its own means and its own spread: a distribution-shift evaluation, not an i.i.d. one.

**Metrics.** Top-1 accuracy (the README calls it exact naming); the negative log likelihood of the true class, NLL in nats, the proper scoring rule the selection is made on; the expected calibration error, ECE, of the top probability in ten bins; and selective-classification numbers at the 0.99 threshold the rule uses for a confident answer: coverage (how often the top probability reaches 0.99) and precision (how often such an answer is right).
protocol:
**Outer loop: leave-one-population-out.** Each of the 22 papers that print at least one measure at every lumbar level that another paper also prints is held out in turn. The candidate classifiers are built from the other papers alone, including every pooled statistic they read (the between-population spread tau is re-estimated without the held-out paper). 1,000 synthetic columns of five lumbar bodies are drawn from the held-out paper's table, giving 5,000, 4,000 and 3,000 fields at one, two and three bodies, and every candidate is scored on the same fields, so comparisons are paired. The held-out populations are the same draws, on the same seeds, as the stats page's strata study.

**Inner loop: nested cross-validation for the hyperparameters.** Two candidates have a knob. The SD factor k multiplies every SD of the pooled table (k = 1 is the plain rule); the temperature T divides the log evidence before the softmax over classes (T = 1 is the exact posterior; this is temperature scaling, which changes confidence and never the argmax). For each outer fold the knobs are chosen on the training papers alone: each training paper that prints any of the held-out paper's measures is in turn held out of the rest, 150 columns are drawn from it, and the rule built on the rest is scored over the grid k in {0.7 ... 3.0} and T in {0.5 ... 8}. k maximises the mean inner log score over folds and widths; T is chosen per width. The held-out paper is dropped from the training cells entirely before the inner loop, so nothing of it reaches the choice.

**Candidates.** Plain: the pooled means and within-person SDs as the rule uses them today. Widened: the SD inflated to sqrt(sd^2 + tau^2 + SE^2), the posterior predictive spread of one more population's mean under the hierarchy, with no knob. Scaled: SD times k, k from the inner loop. Tempered: plain with T from the inner loop. Mixture: one component per training paper, the pool with that paper's own cells substituted where it prints them, equal weights, the evidence averaged over components (Bayesian model averaging over the populations seen). The held-out paper's own table is scored beside them as the oracle: the best any classifier of this family could do on that population.

**Statistics.** Each held-out population is one fold with equal weight. A candidate's number is its mean over the 22 folds with the SE across folds; its difference from plain is the paired difference per fold, with its SE across folds and the count of folds it wins. Choosing the best of five candidates on the same folds is a small selection and is said as such; each candidate's own number is honest.
result:
**Winner by held-out NLL: temperature scaling with T = 2.** Dividing the plain rule's log evidence by 2 before the softmax lowers the held-out NLL from 1.431, 1.243 and 0.957 nats at one, two and three bodies to 1.342, 1.127 and 0.849, a paired 0.090, 0.116 and 0.108 below plain (SE over folds 0.049 to 0.065), and wins 15, 17 and 16 of the 22 folds. Top-1 accuracy is untouched by construction. Half of the mean gain comes from one fold, Yadav 2020 (1.07 to 1.28 nats), whose people spread twice as wide as the training pool; without it the gain is 0.043 to 0.053 (SE 0.015 to 0.020) on 14 to 16 of 21 folds. ECE falls from 0.094, 0.110 and 0.101 to 0.020, 0.037 and 0.039. The inner CV chose T = 2 on 11 to 13 of the 22 folds, 1.4 on 6 to 8 and 2.8 on 1 to 4, and the held-out curve over T bottoms at 2 at every width, so the nested choice lands on the held-out optimum (panel E).

**Runner-up: variance inflation by tau, no hyperparameter.** NLL 0.058, 0.076 and 0.064 below plain (SE 0.030 to 0.041), ECE 0.027 to 0.042, accuracy unchanged. It is what the hierarchical model says the predictive SD of a new population is, so it needs no inner loop.

**The SD factor k** chosen by inner CV (1.45 on 14 of 22 folds, where the held-out curve bottoms too, panel D) gains 0.028 to 0.047 nats but costs 0.4 to 0.9 points of accuracy: one factor for every cell is wrong for the held-out population more often than the cell's own tau is.

**The mixture** (Bayesian model averaging over the other papers' tables, equal prior weights) is the only candidate that raises accuracy, by 0.4, 0.3 and 0.5 points (SE 0.3): 5.0 points on Yu 2015, 3.3 on Arockiaraj 2025 and Otsuki 2021 at three bodies, 1 to 2 points down on Olsewski 1990 and Griffith 2016. Its NLL is only 0.007 to 0.021 below plain and its ECE 0.069 to 0.089: every component is as confident as the pool, so averaging them leaves the overconfidence.

**Selective classification at 0.99.** Tempered answers on 1.1, 2.2 and 3.1% of fields (plain 3.7, 6.4 and 10.1) with precision 99, 90 and 91%; Yadav 2020 holds 170 of its 178 errors at three bodies, and with that fold apart the precision is 99.9, 99.6 and 99.5% against plain's 96.3, 96.6 and 95.5% and widened's 98.8 to 99.1%.

**The ceiling.** The oracle, the held-out population's own table, is 0.29 to 0.37 nats and 9 to 12 accuracy points better than any candidate at every width. That gap is mean shift between populations: no change to the variances, the temperature or the component set recovers it, only data from the target population would. Choosing the best of five on the same 22 folds is a mild selection; each candidate's own number is honest, and the winner's margin over plain holds on every width and without its best fold.
verdict:
- **Ship temperature scaling, T = 2.** One division of the log evidence before the softmax, at every width. It changes no argmax, lowers held-out NLL by about 0.1 nats, brings ECE to 0.02 to 0.04 and makes the 0.99 label honest on every population whose spread is within twice the pool's. Chosen by nested leave-one-population-out, and the held-out curve agrees.
- **Keep variance inflation by tau as the fallback with no hyperparameter**, nearly as good, and the obvious combination to test next: widened then tempered, with T re-chosen by the inner loop.
- **Do not expect accuracy gains from reweighting.** Every candidate names within a point of the plain rule; the 9 to 12 point gap to the oracle is distribution shift of the means. The only lever is target-population data, or the population register's strata as the mixture's components once pull request 43 lands, so a field is scored against the populations it resembles.
- **Treat Yadav 2020 as out of distribution**, not as a rule problem: its printed SDs are 2.1 times every other population's, so its confident answers are wrong 3 times in 10 under every candidate.
- Nothing in schwingcheck's rule is changed by this note; carrying the temperature is the owner's call.

fig14_strata.how_to_read: Leave-one-population-out before any knob was tuned. A: one row a held-out paper, x the accuracy drop in points against its own table (the oracle) at three bodies, under the pooled rule (filled), the widened rule (squares) and a diagnostic ablation, the paper's own means with the pool's SDs (triangles), which isolates the part of the drop caused by the spread mismatch alone; the diamond is the random-effects mean over folds with the predictive interval for a new population. B: the drop by field width. C: precision of the 0.99 answers. D: populations sampled from the hierarchy itself.
fig14_strata.what_it_shows: Domain shift costs 8.8 points of accuracy at one body and 12.2 at three, with a between-fold SD of 7 to 8 points, so a new population can lose anything from nothing to about 30. Only 2 to 4 of those points come from the SD mismatch; the rest is mean shift, which no variance inflation can recover. The plain rule is overconfident off-distribution: its 0.99 answers are right 87 to 92% of the time, and on populations sampled from the hierarchy only 83 to 86% at two and three bodies; the widened rule brings that to 100% there and to 99% on every real paper but Yadav 2020, at the price of answering half as often.

fig12_naming_measures.how_to_read: A feature-count curve, in-distribution (test columns are drawn from the same table the rule reads, so this is the i.i.d. ceiling, not the held-out number). Along the bottom the number of measures the classifier reads, from the seven SPINEPS measures through the generator's 32 to every complete measure of the table; up the side top-1 accuracy. A is the whole column C3 to L5, B the lumbar run. Solid lines at the generator's setting, dotted at the setting nearest the papers.
fig12_naming_measures.what_it_shows: More features help a lot in distribution: one body of the whole column is named right 47.3% of the time on seven measures, 87.2% on 32 and 89.0% on 35; three bodies 72.8, 98.3 and 98.9%. Over the lumbar run one body reaches 97.6% on the papers' 62 complete measures. The i.i.d. ceiling is therefore high, and the held-out populations above are where the real loss sits.

fig5_naming.how_to_read: A robustness sweep over the simulator's hyperparameters, one at a time (its state space): the size spread, the within-person correlation rho, neighbour correlation phi, correlation between measures, the measurement error, the SD scale. Panels are fields of one, three and nine bodies; up the side top-1 accuracy on the seven SPINEPS measures; filled markers are the rule built for the generator's own setting scored on data from each setting (a mismatch test), open ones a rule that knows the setting.
fig5_naming.what_it_shows: Accuracy is most sensitive to the measurement error (doubling the CT's error costs 8 points at one body) and to the population's spread (a narrower population gains 9 to 11 points); the correlation knobs cost almost nothing. At the setting nearest the papers one body is named right 57.1% against 47.5% at the generator's, three bodies 80.2 against 72.8, nine 99.0 against 95.6.

fig1_means.how_to_read: Sim-to-real check of the first moment. One lumbar measure a panel, L1 to L5 along the bottom, millimetres up the side: black circles are the means the simulator is built on (Panjabi's twelve cadavers), open squares the published papers pooled by the hierarchical model with their intervals, grey circles each published series, the grey band the simulator's mean plus or minus one SD.
fig1_means.what_it_shows: The simulator's means sit above the papers' pooled means in the two depths (by 1.3 to 1.4 of its own SD) and the pedicle's width (0.8 to 1.0), within 0.4 SD in the end-plate's width and the canal, and below in the posterior body height; over 421 cells the median offset is 0.69 SD. The offset is one of shape more than of scale, so a global rescaling would not remove it.

fig2_spread.how_to_read: Sim-to-real check of the second moment. A: one column a measure on a log scale, each cell's simulated SD divided by the pooled published SD, the median over levels with the interquartile bar; 1 means the simulator spreads exactly as the papers do. Filled circles are the generator as shipped, open squares with the size factor removed from the source SDs, triangles the setting nearest the papers; Panjabi's own SDs are drawn beside them. B keeps the levels four or more measures reach.
fig2_spread.what_it_shows: The simulator is about 70% too dispersed: a median ratio of 1.71 over 140 cells (1.86 as measured). Most of it is inherited from the twelve-cadaver source table, whose SDs are already 1.51 times the papers' (2.83 for the angles), and the generator's size factor multiplies that. A classifier evaluated only on this simulator would see a harder test distribution than real patients present.

fig7_quality.how_to_read: Validity checks on the generated samples, the data-validation step of the pipeline. A: the share of synthetic vertebrae each indicator flags at the three settings, with the unions at the right: a length or area at or below zero (sign), a value clipped at the floor, an area larger than its bounding rectangle (box), an end-plate under half its rectangle (convex), a canal wider than its transverse processes (inside). Sign and inside are hard constraints no anatomy can break; box and convex hold under allowances. B and C break the box flag out by level and measure.
fig7_quality.what_it_shows: 42.2% of synthetic vertebrae carry a flag at the generator's setting, and 9,998 of 10,000 persons do; most flags are an area larger than its own rectangle (32.3%) because measures are sampled independently given the size; the hard constraints fail in 2.2%. Taking the size factor out of the source SDs brings the union to 25.4% and the setting nearest the papers to 7.1%; the seven measures the rule reads are flagged in 13 of 10,000 persons. For a classifier this matters as label noise would: the test distribution holds impossible examples, though the rule's likelihood treats measures as conditionally independent too, so the mismatch is shared. Curation is counted, never applied.

fig15_select.how_to_read: The model-selection figure. A and B: candidates along the bottom, the oracle (the held-out population's own table) first; held-out NLL in A (lower is better) and top-1 accuracy in B, mean over the 22 folds with one-SE bars, one line per field width. C: the reliability diagram at three bodies over every field of every fold, top probability against the share correct, the dotted diagonal perfect calibration, ECE in the legend. D and E: validation curves, the held-out NLL along the SD factor k and the temperature T, with the inner-CV choices as ticks (the curves are drawn after the fact, never used to choose). F: the winner's log score minus plain on each fold at three bodies, 95% bars clustered by column.
fig15_select.what_it_shows: Temperature scaling with T = 2 has the lowest held-out NLL at every width and the lowest ECE at one body, with accuracy identical to plain; the nested choices sit exactly where the held-out curves bottom (k = 1.45, T = 2), which is what a sound inner CV should give. Variance inflation by tau is close behind with no hyperparameter. The mixture is the only candidate above plain on accuracy, by half a point, and is as overconfident as plain. F shows the gain is broad, 16 of 22 folds, and that one fold, Yadav 2020, carries half of the mean.

fig16_exclusion.how_to_read: A and B: each exclusion candidate down the side, held-out log score (A) and top-1 accuracy (B) minus plain, paired over the 22 folds, bars one SE, one marker per field width; right is better. C: each held-out fold at three bodies, the three untempered candidates minus plain. D: ECE of every candidate, all folds pooled.
fig16_exclusion.what_it_shows: Neither drop improves held-out NLL; each costs the folds that share the dropped paper's measures (the Front. Phys. 2026 fold loses 0.81 nats without Yadav). One vote per population is a wash. Temperature scaling gives the same 0.08 to 0.16 nat gain on top of every variant, and the tempered variants are within 0.012 nats of each other.

fig17_covariates.how_to_read: A: effect of sex on each measure, men minus women in within-sex SDs (Cohen's d with the small-sample correction), estimated inside each paper and then pooled across papers, 95% intervals. B: the same for age per decade and body height and weight. C: AUC of a one-feature classifier for sex (one measure at one known level), filled dots in-population, open squares with the effect transferred from other papers. D: out-of-sample R^2 of the measure given the covariate, in-population against transferred.
fig17_covariates.what_it_shows: Sex is the covariate with signal: in its own population one body measure separates the sexes at AUC up to about 0.9. Held out, the median one-measure AUC is 0.63 against 0.64 in-population, and the best measures keep 0.82 to 0.86 (Tang's end plate, Twomey's disc height). Age carries almost none within adults. The effect's sign transfers between populations and its size only partly.

fig19_bounds.how_to_read: A: one feature (anterior body height) down the column, the band the 95% interval for an unseen domain's mean, with the ideal spine and its lumbar gradient flattened and reversed overlaid. B: pass rate by test (mean, SD, step) for each cohort, the dashed line the step threshold calibrated on held-out papers.
fig19_bounds.what_it_shows: A broken gradient stays inside every per-level band in A, so per-feature bounds alone would accept it; in B only the step test drops below its threshold for the broken spines and for schwingcheck's generator.

fig18_sex_naming.how_to_read: A: synthetic domains, x the true sex shift in within-sex SDs, y the log-score gain from conditioning on sex (nats per field), bars 95%, one line per field width. B: each paper held out, the same gain with g from the other papers only, at the paper's own temperature; grey papers borrow their SDs and stay out of the pooled row; the diamonds at the foot are the pooled headline.
fig18_sex_naming.what_it_shows: The information is real but small: about 0.03 nats at one body for contrasts the size the papers print, shrinking with width. Held out, it vanishes: gains on Yu, Bach and Shin are cancelled by Yadav 2020, an out-of-distribution domain, and the pooled interval straddles zero at every width.

fig20_gold3.how_to_read: A: pass rate by test and feature family for each real cohort; dashed, the threshold from held-out papers; dotted, their median. B and D: per feature, the grey bar is the card's 95% interval for an unseen domain's sex effect (B) or age slope (D), the tick its centre, the markers the two cohorts. C: pedicle width down the column, the card's band against the engine's values.
fig20_gold3.what_it_shows: Body and end-plate steps pass and sex effects sit mostly inside their intervals; the disc and pedicle steps fail, and C shows why: the engine's pedicle width leaves the papers' band from L3 down.

exclusion:
**Question.** Should a training population be dropped? Yadav 2020 (302 people) has end-plate SDs 2 to 6 times the only other paper that reports them, Front. Phys. 2026 (20 people). The owner chose on 2026-10-30 to let held-out performance decide rather than drop it by eye.

**Candidates.** The plain rule retrained without Yadav 2020; without Front. Phys. 2026; and with each cell's SD the geometric mean of the training populations' SDs, one vote per population whatever its n. Each also with its own temperature from the inner CV. Same 22 outer folds, same fields, paired.

**Result.** Dropping Yadav raises held-out NLL by 0.041 to 0.053 nats and wins 2 or 3 of 22 folds; the Front. Phys. 2026 fold loses 0.81 nats, since its end-plate prior then comes from Tan 2004 alone. Dropping Front. Phys. 2026 wins 1 fold at each width and costs Busscher 2010, Moncada-Habib 2025 and Tan 2004 0.16 to 0.21 nats. One vote per population is within 0.006 nats of plain. With temperature scaling every variant lands within 0.012 nats of the tempered plain rule (0.849 to 0.861 at three bodies). **Verdict: drop nothing; ship T = 2.**
project:
- **What this feeds.** SchwingCheck names the level of a measured vertebra; its prior over places is the table of means and SDs this report evaluates. The output to carry is that table with its log evidence tempered by T = 2, chosen by nested leave-one-population-out. Whether schwingcheck's rule carries the temperature is the owner's call; nothing here changes it.
- **Covariates, from the literature.** Read within each paper, then pooled over 22 papers that print men and women apart: men exceed women by about 1.3 within-sex SDs on the vertebral body, 0.5 to 0.7 on the pedicle, 0.45 on the canal's width and nothing on its depth; age moves a measure by under 0.2 SD a decade. Held out by paper (20 papers, 357 strata), one measure predicts sex at median AUC 0.63 against the domain's own 0.64 and NLL 0.680 against the base rate's 0.693; the effect's sign transfers in 85% of strata, its size only partly.
- **Covariates, per person.** The real test is a classifier trained on people, not papers: the gold tier 3 CTs measured by bordercall's morphometry on the grid, with each person's age and sex. The join ran (job 40878978) and printed per-sex moments for autoPET (857 adults) and TotalSegmentator (133); VerSe's 21 got no sex. Its effects are read against the card in Real CTs on the card; a per-person classifier needs the per-person table, which stays on the grid. Any grid job waits for the owner's word and job count.
- **Next model.** A population-conditioned prior: the mixture over populations with the covariates as the component weights, so a field's posterior also says which population, sex or age band it resembles. That is the next candidate for the same held-out protocol.
bounds:
**Question.** Can the published tables serve as bounds for a generative model of spines? Yes, as an acceptance test a synthetic cohort must pass (synthval/bounds.py, the owner's question of 2026-10-30, 03:38 UTC).

**The test.** For each feature (53 measures, 694 measure-level cells) and each adjacent-level difference (635 steps), a 95% predictive interval for an unseen domain's mean, SD and step: the random-effects pool plus or minus 1.96 sqrt(SE^2 + tau^2), tau the between-paper spread. Steps are read inside each paper first, so a paper's own offset cancels. A cohort passes when its pass rate on each test reaches the threshold, and the step test must pass, since naming reads the steps.

**Threshold, calibrated on held-out domains.** Each of 33 papers left out, scored on the card of the rest; the threshold is the 10th percentile of their pass rates (means 0.58, SDs 0.53, steps 0.89). Those papers measured about 40 people (median 44), so every cell is scored at an effective sample size of 40: a cohort of thousands would otherwise face tighter intervals than the real domains the threshold came from.

**Result.** The ideal spine (the card's centre) passes. The same spine with its lumbar gradient flattened or reversed fails on steps (0.87, 0.79) while its means pass, so the step test is the discriminating one. schwingcheck's generator on Panjabi's table fails (steps 0.86, means 0.70), as does the grid point nearest the papers (steps 0.80). Of 200 domains sampled from the card's own model, 175 pass; the 25 that fail do so on 188 steps whose two levels' intervals cannot both be honoured.

**Use.** As an acceptance test, as a loss term (mean squared z over cells: about 1 in distribution, 3.4 for schwingcheck's generator), and, with each person's sex given, as a sign check on the sex contrast. It cannot bound one person's cross-feature correlation (no paper prints it), anomalies such as L6 or T13, or populations no paper sampled.
sex_naming:
**Question.** The patient's sex is known at imaging time (the owner, 2026-10-30, 03:45 UTC). Does giving it to the classifier as an input improve naming of a 1-, 2- or 3-body field? Exploratory, not pre-registered.

**Setup.** Paired comparison on the same fields: rule A is the sexless class-conditional table; rule B conditions each class's Gaussian on the given sex (mean shifted by the sex contrast g, SD narrowed to within-sex). Held out: leave-one-paper-out over 18 papers that print men and women apart; A is the other papers' table at the held-out paper's own temperature (chosen by the same inner CV as before), B the same table conditioned on sex with g estimated from the other papers only. Headline over the 16 papers with printed SDs. Ceilings, which no deployable rule reaches: the held-out paper's own g, and its own per-sex tables.

**Result, held out.** Conditioning on sex changes held-out log score by +0.001, -0.003 and -0.003 nats at 1, 2 and 3 bodies (SE 0.006 to 0.009) and top-1 accuracy by +0.1 to +0.2 points: no measurable gain. With the target domain's own g it would be +0.007 to +0.011 nats; with the target's own per-sex tables over its own sexless table, +1.0 to +1.7 points. For scale, the target's own sexless table over the other papers' is worth +5.9 to +8.4 points: domain shift is about five times the sex effect.

**Result, synthetic.** Domains split by the papers' own per-cell sex contrasts: +1.9 points at one body, +1.1 at two, +0.1 at three (log score +0.034, +0.025, +0.007 nats).

**Verdict.** Carry sex as an input: it costs nothing in expectation when g matches the domain. Do not expect it to close the gap to the target domain; that takes target-domain data, which the gold tier 3 join (job 40878978, read in Real CTs on the card) is the first to give with each person's sex.
gold3:
**Question.** Do real spines, measured by our morphometry engine, pass the bounds card? Two held-out real cohorts from gold tier 3 answer it: autoPET's 857 adults and TotalSegmentator's 133, each person's sex known (the grid's join, job 40878978, read as per-sex moments; synthval/gold3.py).

**Same protocol as a generator.** Each cohort is scored at an effective sample size of 40 people a cell, against the same thresholds (means 0.58, SDs 0.53, steps 0.89), the step test deciding.

**Result.** Both fail on steps (0.81 each). Split by feature family the failure is the engine's, not the people's: body and end-plate steps pass (0.94, 0.99), disc steps do not (0.74, 0.65), pedicle and canal steps do not (0.66, 0.66). The engine's pedicle features drift from the papers' below L2: pedicle width 27 mm at L5 against 15, chord 27 mm against 44, transverse angle -16 degrees against +23.

**Sex as a covariate is calibrated.** The sex effect (Hedges' g, men minus women) falls inside the card's 95% interval for an unseen domain at 103 of 123 cells and 116 of 127 (84% and 91%), with the papers' sign at 131 of 134 tested cells; the cohorts' effects are slightly smaller (mean z -0.24, -0.70; RMS z 1.34, 1.20, so the intervals are a little narrow). Age slopes are under-covered (18 of 33, 29 of 37): the card's between-domain spread for age is not identified.

**What to do.** Use the card today on body and end-plate steps and on the sex effect; fix the engine's pedicle features below L2 before reading a disc or pedicle failure as the generator's; and use the gold cohorts, measured by the same engine, as a second reference that shares its feature definitions.
